title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 90
paragraphs: When the Lydians came and repeated what they had been enjoined to say, it is related that the Pythian prophetess spoke as follows: “The fated destiny it is impossible even for a god to escape. And Croesus has paid the debt owed for the sin of his fifth ancestor, who, being one of the spearmen of the Heraclidae, followed the treacherous device of a woman, and having slain his master, took possession of his royal dignity, which did not belong to him by right. And although Loxias eagerly desired that the calamity of Sardis might come upon the sons of Croesus and not upon Croesus himself, it was not possible for him to turn the Destinies aside from their course. Yet so much as they granted, he brought to pass and gave as a gift to Croesus: for he put off the taking of Sardis by three years; and let Croesus be assured that he was taken prisoner later by these years than the fated time. And moreover, secondly, he assisted him when he was about to be burned. As to the oracle that was given, Croesus finds fault on good grounds: for Loxias told him beforehand that if he marched against the Persians he would destroy a great empire. And he, on hearing this, if he wished to take counsel well, ought to have sent and asked further whether the god meant his own empire or that of Cyrus. But since he did not comprehend what was said and did not ask again, let him pronounce himself to be the cause of what followed. To him also, when he consulted the Oracle for the last time, Loxias said what he said concerning a mule; but this too he failed to comprehend. For Cyrus was in fact this mule, seeing that he was born of parents of two different races, his mother being of nobler descent and his father of less noble: for she was a Median woman, daughter of Astyages, king of the Medes, while he was a Persian, one of a race subject to the Medes, and being inferior in every respect he was the husband of a woman who was his royal mistress.” Thus the Pythian prophetess replied to the Lydians, and they brought the answer back to Sardis and repeated it to Croesus; and he, when he heard it, acknowledged that the fault was his own and not the god’s. With regard, then, to the empire of Croesus and the first conquest of Ionia, it happened thus.
